title: Vue 2 and Vue 3 Migration
keywords: Professional Practices, Legacy Projects, and Further Learning
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Vue 2 and Vue 3 Migration in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies Vue 2 and Vue 3 Migration within Professional Practices, Legacy Projects, and Further Learning. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Production work continues after the first successful render: teams need a reproducible workflow for review, upgrades, bug reports, and releases.

content_blocks.title: Vue 2 and Vue 3 Migration: Safe maintenance workflow
content_blocks.alt_text: Safe maintenance workflow diagram for lesson 149: Vue 2 and Vue 3 Migration. Record versions, behavior, and constraints → Add a regression check before migration → Compare behavior and document recovery
content_blocks.caption: Maintenance flow: preserve existing behavior with inventory, incremental changes, repeatable checks, and a rollback plan.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Professional Vue engineering covers maintainable code, version control, documentation, migration, shared UI systems, and responsible community work. This lesson focuses on Vue 2 and Vue 3 Migration. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Identifying Vue 2 applications
items.text: For Identifying Vue 2 applications, inventory current behavior and dependency constraints before changing a legacy project. Make the smallest reversible change, add regression checks, and document why a new convention is safer or easier to maintain.

items.title: Major migration considerations
items.text: For Major migration considerations, inventory current behavior and dependency constraints before changing a legacy project. Make the smallest reversible change, add regression checks, and document why a new convention is safer or easier to maintain.

items.title: Options API compatibility
items.text: For Options API compatibility, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

items.title: Updating dependencies and tooling
items.text: For Updating dependencies and tooling, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

items.title: Testing behavior after migration
items.text: For Testing behavior after migration, define the behavior a user can observe before writing the assertion. Test a typical case and one boundary/failure case, keep dependencies deterministic, and use component or browser tests only when that level adds confidence.

content_blocks.code: Inventory runtime and dependencies → capture current behavior with tests → migrate one area → compare routes and interactions → document rollback.
content_blocks.expected_output: Migration is treated as a sequence of verifiable changes rather than an all-at-once rewrite.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use in a non-production branch with a lockfile and a written rollback plan. Vue 2 and Vue CLI are legacy-maintenance topics in this course.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Vue 2 and Vue 3 Migration with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Major migration considerations”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: Professional Vue engineering covers maintainable code, version control, documentation, migration, shared UI systems, and responsible community work. For Vue 2 and Vue 3 Migration, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Vue 2 and Vue 3 Migration” that applies “Identifying Vue 2 applications”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Identifying Vue 2 applications”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.

Verify a normal result and one meaningful boundary case before using the pattern in a production feature.
